# Impact of long COVID on self-reported disease activity, disability, and quality of life in individuals with inflammatory arthritis

**Authors:** Zachary S. Wallace; Miao Lin; Shruthi Srivatsan; Andrew King; Xiaosong Wang; Rathnam Venkat; Yumeko Kawano; Madison Negron; Buuthien Hang; Abigail Schiff; Jennifer Hanberg; Emily N. Kowalski; Colebrook Johnson; Kathleen M.M. Vanni; Zachary Williams; Grace Qian; Caleb Bolden; Kevin T. Mueller; Katarina J. Bade; Alene A. Saavedra; Naomi J. Patel; Jeffrey A. Sparks

**Affiliations:** 1Division of Rheumatology, Allergy, and Immunology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 2Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 3Division of Rheumatology, Inflammation, and Immunity, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

People with inflammatory arthritis are at risk for poor COVID-19 outcomes. Little is known about the impact of long COVID on disease activity, disability, and quality of life in this population.

We included participants with rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, or axial spondyloarthritis from RheumCARD, a prospective cohort study of people with rheumatic disease with and without prior COVID-19. Long COVID was defined as any symptom of acute COVID-19 for ≥90 days. Surveys include the Routine Assessment of Patient Index Data 3 (RAPID-3), modified health assessment questionnaire (MHAQ), short form-12 (SF-12), fatigue symptom inventory, and short form McGill Pain Questionnaire. We assessed the association of long COVID status with these outcomes.

We analyzed n=59 with long COVID, n=165 without long COVID, and n=59 without prior COVID-19. The most common long COVID symptoms were fatigue (37.3%), altered smell/taste (27.1% and 25.4%), difficulty breathing (20.3%), and headache (15.3%). Those with vs. without long COVID had worse mHAQ (median 0.4 vs. 0.1, p<0.001), RAPID-3 (4.0 vs. 2.3, p=0.0005), and physical and mental health (SF-12: 37.7 vs. 47.2, p=0.0003 and 45.3 vs. 53.0, p=0.003, respectively). Fatigue and pain were worse in those with vs. without long COVID (p<0.05 for comparisons). Similar trends were observed in those with long COVID vs. those without prior COVID-19.

Long COVID may result in worsened pain, fatigue, and quality of life in people with inflammatory arthritis. Interpretation of patient-reported outcomes may be difficult because of the impact of long COVID.

## INTRODUCTION

People with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), psoriatic arthritis (PsA), axial spondyloarthritis (AxSpA), and juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) experience a wide range of outcomes when infected with SARS-CoV-2(1). Extensive prior work has highlighted the impact of demographics (e.g., older age, race/ethnicity), comorbidities (e.g., interstitial lung disease), and immunosuppressive treatments (e.g., glucocorticoids, rituximab) on an increased risk of poor acute COVID-19 outcomes in people living with these conditions(2). Many of the immunosuppressive treatments used to treat these conditions, particularly glucocorticoids, methotrexate, and rituximab, also impact the effectiveness of SARS-CoV-2 vaccination(3, 4). Collectively, these factors put these patients at risk for COVID-19 and severe acute outcomes(1). However, less is known about the impact of post-acute COVID-19 outcomes on quality of life and self-reported disease activity in people with inflammatory arthritis who report long COVID symptoms(5–7). Indeed, prior reports in this population describe a significant burden of long COVID, defined as the persistence of symptoms of acute SARS-CoV-2 infection beyond the acute phase of infection(8–13). In addition, some reports indicate that COVID-19 may be associated with exacerbation(11, 14) or risk of incident autoimmune diseases(15–20), such as inflammatory arthritis.

Accumulating evidence suggests that in people with and without inflammatory arthritis and other immune-mediated conditions, SARS-CoV-2 has effects on the immune system, including hyperinflammation, autoantibody formation, and dysregulated humoral and cellular responses, that may persist beyond the acute phase of COVID-19. In the context of underlying autoimmune diseases, including inflammatory arthritis and other conditions, such perturbations may have detrimental effects on quality of life and disease activity. Since most people with inflammatory arthritis have experienced at least one COVID-19 infection since the COVID-19 pandemic began in 2020 and as the incidence of new infections remains high, it is important to understand the impact of COVID-19 on this population. Further, the symptoms of long COVID can share features with those of inflammatory arthritis, which may impact the use of general and disease-specific quality of life measures typically used in routine clinical practice to assess disease activity. Little is known about the impact of COVID-19 infection and long COVID on the experience of patients with inflammatory arthritis. Previous work has focused largely on the impact of the pandemic but not infections or their ramifications(21–25) on quality of life in people with inflammatory arthritis.

Therefore, we aimed to assess the quality of life, disease activity, and the burden of pain and fatigue in a prospective cohort of patients with inflammatory arthritis with and without prior COVID-19 infection. We hypothesized that people with inflammatory arthritis who experience long COVID have worse quality of life, higher disease activity, more pain, and more fatigue compared to those without long COVID and those with rheumatic disease without prior COVID-19 infection.

## METHODS

### Study Design and Population

We invited patients with confirmed SARDs at least 28 days after COVID-19 infection to participate in a prospective cohort study, COVID-19 and Rheumatic Diseases (RheumCARD)(13, 26–29). A comparator group of patients with no reported prior history of COVID-19 infection was also invited to participate. Invitations were sent on a rolling basis via the electronic health record (EHR) or by US mail monthly starting on March 11, 2021, as previously detailed(12, 13, 26, 27, 29). This cohort has been previously described, and other outcomes have been reported elsewhere(13, 26–29). We invited people to participate at least 4 weeks after their positive COVID-19 test. This analysis is limited to patients with a history of rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, axial spondyloarthritis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis to reduce potential for heterogeneity across other types of systemic rheumatic disease and because some of the survey instruments, including the mHAQ and RAPID-3, were developed specifically for inflammatory arthritis. We included patients who completed surveys through October 1, 2023. This study was approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board (2020P004059).

### Data collection

The survey collected demographic information (age, sex, race, ethnicity) and details of the COVID-19 infection including diagnosis date, acute COVID-19 symptoms, and symptom duration. Symptoms of COVID-19 evaluated included fatigue/malaise, fever, headache, myalgias, rhinorrhea, cough, anosmia, dysgeusia, sore throat, dyspnea, chest pain, nausea or vomiting, diarrhea, joint pain, new rash, hives, or blisters, and other acute symptoms. Patients reported their DMARD use at the time of COVID-19 infection. Using EHR data, we also assessed whether each individual had any history of fibromyalgia, depression, or anxiety based on the use of at least one ICD-10 billing code associated with these diagnoses in the 12 months prior to the date of COVID-19.

### Definition of ‘long COVID’

Long COVID was defined according to the World Health Organization (WHO), which requires continuation or development of new symptoms at least 90 days after initial SARS-CoV-2 infection, lasting at least 2 months with no other explanation(12, 13, 26, 27, 29). In a sensitivity analysis, we performed analyses based on the original US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), which defined long COVID as symptom duration for at least 28 days. Based on this, we classified RheumCARD participants into one of three mutually exclusive groups: (1) History of COVID-19 infection with long COVID; (2) History of COVID-19 infection without long COVID (<28 days duration); (3) No known history of COVID-19 infection (Comparator). In the primary analysis, we excluded people with persistent COVID-19 symptoms but assessed prior to day 90 after COVID-19 onset. A history of COVID-19 infection was based on documentation of either a positive SARS-CoV-2 antigen or PCR test; this included antigen tests that were performed at home and reported to a provider or their office. Comparators were classified as such if they denied any prior history of COVID-19 infection and had no record of positive SARS-CoV-2 test in the EHR.

### Outcomes

At the time of their initial survey, participants completed the following survey instruments: (1) modified Health Assessment Questionnaire (mHAQ); (2) Routine Assessment of Patient Index Data 3 (RAPID-3); (3) Short-Form-12 (SF-12); (4) Fatigue Symptom Inventory (FSI); and (5) Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire (SF-MPQ). The mHAQ was designed to assess functional status among people with rheumatic disease(30). The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for the mHAQ is 0.25(31). The RAPID-3 is used to assess disease activity across many rheumatic diseases, including the inflammatory arthritides included in this analysis(32). It is a pooled index of the patient-reported function, pain, and global estimate of status from the American College of Rheumatology’s Core Data Set measures for RA(33). Severity, based on the RAPID-3 score, is characterized as follows: ≤3 indicates remission; 3.1–6 indicates low disease activity; 6.1–12 indicates moderate disease activity; and >12 indicates high disease. An MCID of 3.8 for the RAPID-3 has been previously applied(34). The SF-12 is a generic measure of health status that includes 12 items that are summarized as a physical component score (PCS) and mental component score (MCS) based on responses. The FSI includes 14 items to evaluate different aspects of fatigue, including severity, frequency, and interference with daily functioning(35). The SF-MPQ includes 17 items that assess the sensory and affective aspects of pain. MCIDs for the SF-12, FSI, and SF-MPQ have not been established in inflammatory arthritis. In addition to these validated questionnaires, participants were also asked to rate the perceived control of their rheumatic disease before and after COVID-19 infection on a scale of 0–10, with 10 being well-controlled. People with no reported history of COVID-19 were asked to compare their rheumatic disease control at the time of survey to the time at which their COVID-19 test was performed.

### Statistical Analysis

We assessed the association of exposure status (Prior COVID-19 with long COVID; Prior COVID-19 without long COVID; No prior COVID-19) with each measure of quality of life and disease activity. We used quantile regression to compare median mHAQ, RAPID-3, SF-12, and FSI interference scores across groups in unadjusted and age-, sex-, and race-adjusted analyses. We used unadjusted and age-, sex-, and race-adjusted Poisson regression to compare median scores for the FSI average fatigue scale and the SF-MPQ scales. In the first sensitivity analysis, we analyzed people with the alternative long COVID definition as lasting 28 days or more that is less stringent than the definition used in the primary analysis (symptoms lasting 90 days or longer and meeting WHO critiera). In the second sensitivity analysis, we repeated these analyses after limiting the cohort to those participants with rheumatoid arthritis since that was the most common form of inflammatory arthritis included in this study. In a second sensitivity analysis using the full inflammatory arthritis cohort, we adjusted for depression in addition to age, sex, and race, because of observed differences in the distribution of depression, anxiety, and fibromyalgia across groups; we only included depression as a covariate in these analyses because of the co-linearity of these three conditions.

Statistical significance was set at two-sided p<0.05, and all statistical analyses were completed in the SAS statistical software (V.9.4; SAS Institute).

## RESULTS

### Study Sample and Baseline Characteristics

We analyzed 59 participants with prior COVID-19 who reported long COVID, 165 with prior COVID-19 and no long COVID (symptoms resolved within 28 days), and 59 comparators who had no known history of COVID-19 infection (Table 1).

The mean (SD) age was similar across groups (52.5 [14.8], 53.7 [15.0], and 58.3 [19.3], respectively, p=0.2). There was a trend toward a higher proportion of females in the group with vs those without long COVID and vs. comparators (91.5%, 74.6%, and 78.0%). Most patients in each group were white (84.8%, 89.1%, and 93.2%). RA was the most common diagnosis across groups (76.3%, 64.9%, and 84.8%, p=0.06). Methotrexate (27.1%, 33.3%, and 27.1%) and/or TNF inhibitors (30.5%, 36.4%, and 35.6%) were the most frequently used medications across groups, and a minority in each group were using glucocorticoids (18.6%, 11.5%, 15.3%). Participants who experienced long COVID were more likely to have been infected earlier in the pandemic whereas those without long COVID tended to have been infected by the Omicron variant. Rates of vaccination prior to infection were higher in those without long COVID than in those with long COVID (67.9% vs 33.9%).

### Quality of Life and Disease Activity: Long COVID vs. No Long COVID

Compared to patients without long COVID, those with long COVID had worse measures of disease activity and quality of life (Table 2). After adjustment for age, sex, and race, the median mHAQ was 0.31 (95%CI 0.23, 0.39, p<0.0001) points higher in those with vs. without long COVID. The median RAPID-3 was 1.70 (95%CI 0.87, 2.53, p<0.0001) points higher in those with vs without long COVID. Both the physical component score and the mental health component score of the SF-12 were worse in those with vs. without long COVID (adjusted differences −7.25 [95%CI −10.42, −4.07], p<0.0001 and −4.79 [95%CI −8.53, −1.014], p=0.0126, respectively).

### Long COVID vs. Comparators Without Prior COVID-19

When compared to those without prior COVID-19, the direction of our effect estimates remained similar to the differences among those with and without long COVID. In general, those with long COVID had worse disease control and quality of life (Table 2). The RAPID-3 was higher in those with long COVID than those without prior COVID-19 (adjusted difference 1.70, 95%CI 0.48, 2.92, p=0.0071). The SF-12 mental health component score was also lower in those with long COVID (−7.68, 95%CI −12.76, −2.59, p=0.0035). The average fatigue score was worse in those with long COVID (RR 1.48, 95%CI 1.22, 1.79, p<0.0001). Also, mHAQ was statistically higher (adjusted difference 0.21, 95%CI 0.04, 0.39, p=0.0186).

### Specific Symptoms of Long COVID

Those with long COVID reported a variety of symptoms associated with their SARS-CoV-2 infection that persisted for at least 90 days (Supplemental Table 1). The most common symptoms included fatigue (22, 27.3%), loss of smell (16, 27.1%), altered sense of taste (15, 25.4%), difficulty breathing (12, 20.3%), and headache (9, 15.3%).

### Sensitivity Analyses

Our findings remained similar in analyses with the alternative long COVID definition of 28+ days of symptom duration (Supplemental Tables 2–4), limited to participants with RA (Supplemental Tables 5–7) and after additionally adjusting for baseline depression (Supplemental Table 8). Those without long COVID had similar quality of life, pain, fatigue and self-reported disease activity compared to those with no prior history of COVID-19 infection (Supplemental Tables 9 and 10).

## DISCUSSION

In this study of patients with rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, axial spondyloarthritis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis, we found that long COVID was associated with worse quality of life, pain, fatigue, and self-reported disease activity. Those with a history of COVID-19 but no symptoms of long COVID had similar outcomes compared to those with no history of COVID-19. Collectively, our findings suggest that SARS-CoV-2 may trigger a process in some patients with inflammatory arthritis that exacerbates pain and fatigue and reduces quality of life. Our observations highlight the potential difficulties in interpreting patient-reported outcome measures, even many months after COVID-19, because of the impact of persistent symptoms that began with the SARS-CoV-2 infection. Participants with long COVID reported a significant worsening of the control of their inflammatory arthritis after COVID-19, suggesting that patients and clinicians may struggle to differentiate symptoms of long COVID with those of the underlying inflammatory arthritis. However, participants who recovered without long COVID had similar patient-reported outcomes as comparators who never had COVID-19; this finding provides some reassurance that inflammatory arthritis disease control may not be affected by an acute SARS-CoV-2 infection that resolves within 28 days.

While the factors driving long COVID remain complex and multifactorial, the associations of long COVID with poor self-reported outcomes have been well-described(6). However, little is known about these associations in people living with different forms of inflammatory arthritis who generally have worse quality of life, greater pain, and greater fatigue than the general population. Some people with inflammatory arthritis also have fibromyalgia which has overlap with some of the manifestations (e.g., joint pain, myalgia, fatigue) of long COVID(36). Our findings persisted even after adjusting for a history of depression which correlated with anxiety and fibromyalgia. Additional studies are needed to understand the similarities and differences between the long COVID-19 syndrome, which has diverse manifestations, and fibromyalgia as well as with other conditions, including chronic fatigue syndrome, that share similar characteristics.

The differences between the groups with and without long COVID were greater than the minimal clinically-important differences (MCID) for the mHAQ, highlighting the multi-dimensional impact that long COVID continues to have on this vulnerable population. There is currently no specific treatment for long COVID, though multi-disciplinary approaches to care, guided in part by the person’s manifestations of long COVID, are recommended at this time(37). Ongoing and planned clinical trials are evaluating a variety of potential treatments, including antivirals, intravenous immunoglobulin, structured physical activity, and others. Given the overlap of long COVID symptoms with those of inflammatory arthritis (e.g., pain, fatigue), it is important that the patient’s rheumatologist be involved to ensure that these symptoms are not due to underlying active rheumatic disease.

Though developed and validated in people with inflammatory arthritis, the mHAQ and RAPID-3 do not distinguish whether symptoms and limitations in function are a result of an underlying inflammatory arthritis. We asked participants about their perception of the activity of their inflammatory arthritis. Indeed, those with long COVID reported worse control of their inflammatory arthritis than those without long COVID and those who never had COVID-19. Future studies are needed to objectively assess disease activity (e.g., tender and swollen joint counts, circulating markers of inflammation) in inflammatory arthritis and its associations with long COVID. Such studies are critical since self-perceived worsening of disease control may lead to unnecessary switching or discontinuation of effective disease modifying anti-rheumatic drugs.

The RAPID-3 and mHAQ questionnaires are commonly used in day-to-day practice as a measure of disease control and function(38). Indeed, their assessment is used to measure quality of care and is required in some settings to ensure reimbursement or to justify management decisions. It is therefore critical for clinicians and payers to understand the factors that may impact these measures. Whether the differences in RAPID-3 and mHAQ that we observed between patients with and without long COVID reflect poorly controlled inflammatory arthritis or non-inflammatory manifestations of long COVID requires further investigation.

There are several potential explanations for our findings. First, the immunologic perturbations associated with COVID-19 may contribute to flares of underlying inflammatory arthritis(19, 29, 39–43). Second, these immunologic sequelae may lead to systemic inflammation and non-inflammatory manifestations of long COVID. Third, patients are generally counseled to hold immunosuppressive therapies in the context of an acute COVID-19 infection(27). Prolonged discontinuation of these therapies may lead to flares of disease activity that may be difficult to control, even with resumption of prior treatment regimens. Fourth, persistent SARS-CoV-2 antigenemia has been identified in sites outside of the respiratory tract and this could contribute to our findings(44). Further, we previously found that people on certain forms of immunosuppression have a prolonged duration of viral shedding(45). Whether persistent infection occurs at a higher frequency in patients receiving immunosuppressive medications or whether persistent SARS-CoV-2 antigen in the joints or other musculoskeletal sites may be driving our findings needs further study.

Our study has a number of strengths. We prospectively identified people with prevalent inflammatory arthritis and confirmed COVID-19 and recruited them into RheumCARD. We administered validated patient-reported outcome measures in this patient population. Despite these strengths, our study also has certain limitations. First, the majority of patients in our cohort were white and non-Hispanic. The generalizability of our findings to people of other racial and ethnic groups requires further study. Second, we included people with four types of inflammatory arthritis in this analysis. Though these conditions differ from one another in many ways (e.g., underlying biology, common comorbidities), there are important similarities which motivated us to analyze them together. These include shared treatments, manifestations, and outcome measures. Reassuringly, in the subgroup of patients with RA, our findings remained consistent with the overall findings. Additional studies are needed to investigate these outcomes in patients with other systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases. Third, while we observed differences in patient-reported measures of disease activity and other outcomes across groups, we do not know if these correlate with differences in objective measures of rheumatic disease activity. While we carefully phenotyped inflammatory arthritis patients with and without long COVID as well as comparators without COVID-19, it is possible some of the differences may have been due to organ damage from the viral infection rather than long COVID. Nonetheless, our findings highlight the impact of COVID-19 on this vulnerable population and highlight important directions for future research. The prevalence and distribution of specific symptoms was different than studies in the general population. For example, while fatigue was the most common symptom, only 37% of those who met the long COVID definition reported fatigue, which is typically higher in long COVID studies in the general population. We speculate that our study sample of people with inflammatory arthritis who have high rates of baseline pain and fatigue may be less likely to ascribe those symptoms to long COVID rather than new symptoms such as altered taste that were not features of their pre-existing rheumatic disease.

Fourth, the comparator group consisted of people who denied a known history of COVID-19; it is possible that some had a history of asymptomatic or unrecognized COVID-19. Despite this, we found important differences between this group and those with known COVID-19 infections. Fifth, we relied on surveys to obtain patient-reported outcome measures. Serologic markers of inflammation may be more objective and could identify biologic pathways, but blood testing before and after COVID-19 was not available on all participants. Finally, we did not have access to pre-infection patient-reported outcome measures, and we therefore cannot assess the change in the self-reported outcomes before and after COVID-19 infection. It is possible that unmeasured confounding could explain the observed differences. Interestingly, participants in all three exposure groups in this study reported similar levels of inflammatory arthritis disease control prior to their infection or COVID-19 test.

In conclusion, we found that people with inflammatory arthritis and long COVID following COVID-19 infection have worse quality of life and self-reported disease activity and disability than those without long COVID or those without a history of COVID-19 infection. Additionally, they experience greater pain and fatigue. Further studies are needed to elucidate the factors driving these findings and to identify effective management strategies.
